messages.subject: rmr 2.1 Sorts Key Incorrectly
parts:
I discovered rmr 2.1 sorts keys incorrectly but it's okay on rmr 2.0.2. Note "Continental" (below) is in the wrong position.

# SIMPLE WORD COUNT
library(rmr2)
from.dfs(
mapreduce(
input = to.dfs(row.names(mtcars)),
map = function(.,words) 
keyval(unlist(strsplit(words,'\\s+')),1),
reduce = function(word, count) 
keyval(word, sum(count))
)
)

messages.author: 6ac7e7dfbe4f6c38
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#608] Re: rmr 2.1 Sorts Key Incorrectly
parts:
You don't seem to be familiar with the concept of a Hash Partitioner. That's the default in mapreduce (independent of rmr) and because of that keys get randomly scattered around. Plus R objects are just raw bytes to Java, so whatever Java sorting does to them, it's not what you would expect. But in any event it's within reduce groups, not global. If you need global sorting, like in the terasort paper, you need custom partitioners (in that case a Range Partitioner). Unfortunately rmr2 doesn't support those yet. If you know how to implement them, please send your patches our way.


Antonio

Sometimes if the results are small enough, I'll sort results by forcing the number of reducers to 1 - therefore relying on the sort and shuffle phase.

-Alton

On Thursday, February 28, 2013 9:41:06 PM UTC-8, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
You don't seem to be familiar with the concept of a Hash Partitioner. That's the default in mapreduce (independent of rmr) and because of that keys get randomly scattered around. Plus R objects are just raw bytes to Java, so whatever Java sorting does to them, it's not what you would expect. But in any event it's within reduce groups, not global. If you need global sorting, like in the terasort paper, you need custom partitioners (in that case a Range Partitioner). Unfortunately rmr2 doesn't support those yet. If you know how to implement them, please send your patches our way.


Antonio


On Thu, Feb 28, 2013 at 9:18 PM, Alton Ing <al...@altoning.com> wrote:
Sorting keys is one of the core features of the MapReduce "Sort and Shuffle" phase that many design patterns depend on to function properly. I hope this issue will get resolved soon.

-Alton


On Thursday, February 28, 2013 9:11:24 PM UTC-8, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
Hi,
while I am a little surprised by the change of behavior and I will look into it, there is no sorting guarantee, neither in the documentation nor in the tests. If there is, it's a mistake.

Antonio


On Thu, Feb 28, 2013 at 11:48 AM, Jim Solderitsch <jsolde...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have seen similar behavior in my airlines data experiments -- there is an out-of-order key at the end of the key set. This is with 2.1.0 as well.

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#615] Re: rmr 2.1 Sorts Key Incorrectly
parts:
This is what I found
  1. The order Hadoop produces is a raw byte order (all R data goes through Hadoop as raw bytes). Because of the specific serialization used, the strings are sorted short to long first, then alphanumeric within the same length. To verify this, you can run a job with the number of reducers set to 1, but with reduce = NULL argument to mapreduce. This will use a Java identity reducer.
  2. 2.0.2 hides this sort order in smaller examples, but it can't for bigger ones where not all data can be read in memory at once, which is actually the general case. 2.1 never hides this because the last key is processed separately.
  3. A way to have Hadoop follow a more natural oder for at least the simplest types would be to write a custom comparator in Java that skips the first 5 bytes which contain type code and length. I read reports that somebody did something similar for the Dumbo project, with which we share the serialization format, but they didn't share the code.

Antonio

On Thursday, February 28, 2013 9:41:06 PM UTC-8, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
You don't seem to be familiar with the concept of a Hash Partitioner. That's the default in mapreduce (independent of rmr) and because of that keys get randomly scattered around. Plus R objects are just raw bytes to Java, so whatever Java sorting does to them, it's not what you would expect. But in any event it's within reduce groups, not global. If you need global sorting, like in the terasort paper, you need custom partitioners (in that case a Range Partitioner). Unfortunately rmr2 doesn't support those yet. If you know how to implement them, please send your patches our way.


Antonio
